records.topic: What If Your Heart Stopped in Ice Water?
records.hook: Her heart stopped for 2 hours and 35 minutes.
records.openingLine: Her heart stopped for 2 hours and 35 minutes.
records.secondBeat: She was trapped under ice for 80 minutes.
records.scientificMechanism: deep accidental hypothermia slows the body's oxygen demand, so a cold body in circulatory arrest can sometimes be rewarmed on a bypass machine and restarted
records.scenarioChange: a person's heart stopped while trapped under ice in freezing water
records.expectedConsequence: slow rewarming of the blood outside the body restarted the heart and allowed an almost full recovery
records.coreQuestion: If your heart stopped in ice water, could cold keep you alive?
records.misconception: A heart stopped by deep cold isn't always the end.
visualScenes: skier falling onto a frozen stream
editorialTitles: The Skier Whose Heart Stopped for Hours
How Ice Water Saved a Stopped Heart

sources.name: PubMed — Gilbert et al., Lancet 2000: Resuscitation from accidental hypothermia of 13.7 °C with circulatory arrest

facts.claim: Anna Elisabeth Johansson Bågenholm (born 1970) is a Swedish radiologist from Vänersborg, who survived after a skiing accident in 1999 left her trapped under a layer of ice for 80 minutes in freezing water.
facts.quote: left her trapped under a layer of ice for 80 minutes in freezing water

facts.claim: During this time she experienced extreme hypothermia and her body temperature decreased to 13.7 °C (56.7 °F), one of the lowest survived body temperatures ever recorded in a human with accidental hypothermia.
facts.quote: her body temperature decreased to 13.7 °C (56.7 °F)

facts.claim: At first Bågenholm struggled in the cold water before she found an air pocket and was able to remain conscious for 40 minutes before experiencing circulatory arrest.
facts.quote: found an air pocket and was able to remain conscious for 40 minutes

facts.claim: She had no heart beat for 2 hours 35 minutes, from 19:40 till 22:15.
facts.quote: She had no heart beat for 2 hours 35 minutes

facts.claim: At 21:40, she was connected to a cardiopulmonary bypass machine that warmed up her blood outside of her body before it was reinserted into her veins.
facts.quote: connected to a cardiopulmonary bypass machine that warmed up her blood outside of her body

facts.claim: Although she has made an almost full recovery from the incident, late in 2009 she was still having minor symptoms in hands and feet related to nerve injury.
facts.quote: Although she has made an almost full recovery from the incident

facts.claim: Her body became trapped under the ice, which was 20 centimetres (7.9 in) thick.
facts.quote: Her body became trapped under the ice

facts.claim: When Bågenholm was pulled out of the water, her pupils were dilated, her blood was not circulating, and she was not breathing.
facts.quote: her blood was not circulating, and she was not breathing

facts.claim: After rescue, Bågenholm was transported by helicopter to the Tromsø University Hospital, where a team of more than a hundred doctors and nurses worked in shifts for nine hours to save her life.
facts.quote: more than a hundred doctors and nurses worked in shifts for nine hours

facts.claim: Bågenholm's first heart beat was recorded at 22:15, and her body temperature had risen to 36.4 °C (97.5 °F) at 0:49.
facts.quote: Bågenholm's first heart beat was recorded at 22:15

facts.claim: Bågenholm woke up ten days after the accident, paralyzed from the neck down and subsequently spent two months recovering in an intensive care unit.
facts.quote: Bågenholm woke up ten days after the accident

facts.claim: She fell headfirst onto a layer of ice on a frozen stream near a waterfall, landing on her back.
facts.quote: She fell headfirst onto a layer of ice on a frozen stream

facts.claim: When Falkenberg and Næsheim found Bågenholm, only her feet and skis were above the ice.
facts.quote: only her feet and skis were above the ice

facts.claim: They then tried to dig her out, but their snow shovel could not break through the ice.
facts.quote: their snow shovel could not break through the ice

facts.claim: The rescue helicopter soon arrived and Bågenholm was taken to the Tromsø University Hospital in an hour.
facts.quote: Bågenholm was taken to the Tromsø University Hospital in an hour

narration.text: Her heart stopped for 2 hours and 35 minutes.
She was trapped under ice for 80 minutes.
An air pocket kept her conscious for 40 minutes.
Then her body cooled to 13.7 degrees Celsius.
Deep cold slows how much oxygen the body needs.
Doctors warmed her blood outside her body on a bypass machine.
Her heart restarted, and she almost fully recovered.
So in deep cold, stopped isn't always the end.

records.topic: What If You Left Tardigrades in Open Space?
records.hook: What If You Left Tardigrades in Open Space?
records.openingLine: What If You Left Tardigrades in Open Space?
records.secondBeat: Some animals survived 10 days in open space.
records.scientificMechanism: dried tardigrades enter a 'tun' state with no metabolic activity, which resists vacuum, extreme temperatures and radiation; solar ultraviolet light is what killed most of them
records.scenarioChange: dehydrated tardigrades were exposed to the vacuum and sunlight of low Earth orbit
records.expectedConsequence: vacuum alone barely harmed them, while added solar ultraviolet light killed many
records.coreQuestion: If you left tardigrades in open space, what would actually kill them?
records.misconception: For tardigrades, the vacuum of space isn't the deadly part.
visualScenes: tardigrade curling into a dry tun
editorialTitles: The Animal That Survived Open Space
What Space Can't Do to a Tardigrade

sources.name: NASA — Cell Science-04 (tardigrades on the ISS)
NASA — Houston We Have a Podcast: Water Bears in Space

facts.claim: In 2007, samples of 30 tardigrades and 30 eggs, all dehydrated, were taken on the FOTON-M3 mission and exposed to vacuum, to both vacuum and UVA & B light, or to both vacuum and the full range of solar ultraviolet, for 10 days.
facts.quote: were taken on the FOTON-M3 mission and exposed to vacuum

facts.claim: Vacuum exposure alone had no significant effect on any metric, but, when combined with UV exposure, killed many of the tuns.
facts.quote: Vacuum exposure alone had no significant effect on any metric

facts.claim: In this state, they can go without food or water for several years.
facts.quote: they can go without food or water for several years

facts.claim: Further, in that state they become highly resistant to environmental stresses, including temperatures from as low as −272 °C (−458 °F) to as much as +149 °C (300 °F) (at least for short periods of time), lack of oxygen, vacuum, ionising radiation, and high pressure.
facts.quote: temperatures from as low as −272 °C (−458 °F) to as much as +149 °C (300 °F)

facts.claim: Tardigrades can survive impacts up to about 900 metres per second (3,000 ft/s), and momentary shock pressures up to about 1.14 gigapascals (165,000 psi).
facts.quote: Tardigrades can survive impacts up to about 900 metres per second

facts.claim: They have survived exposure to outer space.
facts.quote: They have survived exposure to outer space

facts.claim: The earliest known fossil is from the Cambrian, some 500 million years ago.
facts.quote: The earliest known fossil is from the Cambrian

facts.claim: Tardigrade DNA is protected from radiation by the Dsup ("damage suppressor") protein.
facts.quote: Tardigrade DNA is protected from radiation by the Dsup

facts.claim: In 2011, tardigrades went on the International Space Station STS-134, showing that they could survive microgravity and cosmic radiation, and should be suitable model organisms.
facts.quote: showing that they could survive microgravity and cosmic radiation

facts.claim: Their eggs and resistant life-cycle stages (cysts and tuns) are small and durable enough to enable long-distance transport, whether on the feet of other animals or by the wind.
facts.quote: durable enough to enable long-distance transport

facts.claim: They are among the most resilient animals known, with individual species able to survive severe conditions – such as exposure to extreme temperatures, extreme pressures (both high and low), air deprivation, radiation, dehydration, and starvation – that would quickly kill most other forms of life.
facts.quote: They are among the most resilient animals known

narration.text: What If You Left Tardigrades in Open Space?
Some animals survived 10 days in open space.
They're tardigrades, and dried out, they curl into a tun.
A tun can go without water for years.
In orbit, vacuum alone had no significant effect.
Adding the Sun's ultraviolet light killed many of them.
Tuns briefly handle −272 to 149 degrees Celsius.
So for a tardigrade, space isn't the killer. Sunlight is.
